title: Given an array of integers, return the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence. Aim for O(n log n).
shortTitle: Longest Increasing Subsequence — O(n log n) patience sort

s1_definition.profdef: Patience-sorting DP that maintains a tails array where tails[k] is the smallest possible tail of an increasing subsequence of length k+1. For each number, binary-search the first tail that is greater than or equal to it and replace it (or append if larger than all). The tails length is the LIS length, computed in O(n log n) time, O(n) space.
s1_definition.analogy: A portfolio analyst at National Bank of India scans a daily price stream and tracks the longest run of rising prices, not necessarily consecutive. She keeps a shelf of candidate runs ordered by their smallest ending value and slots each new price into the tightest fit, which keeps every run as extendable as possible.
s1_definition.oneliner: Keep smallest tails; binary-search the slot; tails length is the LIS.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Patience-sorting DP that maintains a tails array where tails[k] is the smallest possible tail of an increasing subsequence of length k+1. For each number, binary-search the first tail that is greater than or equal to it and replace it (or append if larger than all). The tails length is the LIS length, computed in O(n log n) time, O(n) space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A portfolio analyst at National Bank of India scans a daily price stream and tracks the longest run of rising prices, not necessarily consecutive. She keeps a shelf of candidate runs ordered by their smallest ending value and slots each new price into the tightest fit, which keeps every run as extendable as possible.

**One line to remember:** Keep smallest tails; binary-search the slot; tails length is the LIS.

sections.s2_technical:
Maintain a list called tails. For each number x, binary-search for the leftmost tail that is greater than or equal to x. If none exists, x extends the longest run so append it; otherwise replace that tail with x because a smaller tail keeps future extension easier. For example: `int pos = lowerBound(tails, x); if (pos==tails.size()) tails.add(x); else tails.set(pos, x);`.

The tails array is always sorted, which is exactly why binary search is valid. Note that tails is not the actual subsequence, only a device whose length equals the LIS length; reconstructing the real subsequence needs extra parent pointers.

The time is O(n log n) because each of the n numbers does one binary search, and space is O(n). A senior nuance is that using lower bound gives strictly increasing, while upper bound gives non-decreasing, so the bound choice encodes the strictness requirement.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, a portfolio desk wants the longest stretch of rising closing prices over a period to judge momentum, where the rising days need not be consecutive. This is exactly how Longest Increasing Subsequence works.

Problem 2 — A quadratic scan is too slow on long price histories, so an n-log-n method is required. This is exactly why the patience-sorting tails array with binary search is used.

The mini-project builds a `MomentumAnalyzer`, a `BankLogFormatter`, and a runnable demo.

sections.s5_journey:
The input prices are ten, nine, two, five, three, seven, one hundred one, eighteen.

Step 1: Ten starts the tails as a single run ending at ten.

Step 2: Nine replaces ten because a smaller tail is better, then two replaces nine for the same reason.

Step 3: Five appends to make a run of length two, three replaces five to tighten it, seven appends for length three.

Step 4: One hundred one appends for length four, then eighteen replaces one hundred one to keep the length-four run as low as possible.

Step 5: The tails array ends with length four, which is the answer corresponding to two, three, seven, eighteen.

```text

2026-10-27T01:40:00Z [INFO] Longest increasing run length = 4
2026-10-27T01:40:00Z [INFO] prices → LIS = 4
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The Longest Increasing Subsequence in n-log-n time uses patience sorting. I keep a tails array where the entry at index k is the smallest possible tail value of an increasing subsequence of length k plus one. For each number I binary-search the first tail that is greater than or equal to it; if there is none I append the number because it extends the longest run, otherwise I replace that tail with the number because a smaller tail keeps future extension easier.

The tails array stays sorted at all times, which is what makes the binary search valid, and the final length of tails equals the length of the longest increasing subsequence. It is important to understand that tails is not the actual subsequence, only a length device; rebuilding the real subsequence needs parent pointers. Using the lower bound gives a strictly increasing result, while the upper bound would allow equal values.

In my project at National Bank of India, the portfolio desk needed the longest stretch of rising closing prices to judge momentum, and those rising days did not have to be consecutive. The naive quadratic approach was too slow on long histories, so I used this patience-sorting method with binary search to get the answer in n-log-n time.
